entities.label: Idea
entities.summary:
Trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs) represent a vast class of celestial bodies orbiting the Sun at an average distance greater than Neptune, primarily located within the Kuiper Belt and the more distant Oort Cloud. Their significance in the arc of world history lies not in direct human interaction, but in fundamentally reshaping humanity's understanding of our solar system's formation, composition, and the very definition of a 'planet.' The scientific quest to map and characterize these distant, icy worlds began in earnest in the late 20th century, driven by advancements in telescopic technology and theoretical predictions of a substantial reservoir of primordial material beyond the gas giants.

The initial detection of Pluto in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh, though later reclassified, marked the first major discovery of a TNO. Subsequent technological leaps, particularly the development of charge-coupled device (CCD) cameras and automated survey techniques in the 1990s, catalyzed a deluge of discoveries. The 1992 detection of (15760) Albion (formerly 1992 QB1) by David Jewitt and Jane Luu confirmed the existence of the Kuiper Belt, a region teeming with small, icy bodies. This was followed by the identification of numerous dwarf planets such as Eris (discovered 2005), Makemake, and Haumea, many of which rivaled or exceeded Pluto in size, precipitating the intense scientific debate that led to Pluto's reclassification as a dwarf planet in 2006 by the International Astronomical Union (IAU).
